claims.text: The initial single-phase fcc FeCoNi or closely matched derivative has high saturation magnetization and coercivity at or below 100 Oe.
Low-temperature annealing of fcc FeCoNi can induce precipitation or decomposition.
The annealing-induced precipitates in FeCoNi can be controlled at the nanoscale.
Annealing at approximately 550°C for a calibrated duration followed by rapid quenching is an appropriate treatment for producing the proposed microstructure.
An annealing window exists that is sufficient to nucleate nanoscale precipitates but avoids a full phase transformation of fcc FeCoNi.
Nanoscale precipitates or ordered clusters can form within an overall fcc FeCoNi matrix.
The precipitates or ordered clusters provide localized regions of enhanced magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Annealing triggers heterogeneous nucleation of the proposed nanoprecipitates.
The nanoprecipitates act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Enhanced domain-wall pinning increases resistance to magnetic-domain reversal and therefore increases coercivity.
The annealed alloy will have coercivity substantially above 100 Oe relative to the as-synthesized control.
The annealed alloy will largely retain the high saturation magnetization of the fcc matrix.
The intervention is effective only while precipitates remain nanoscale and the overall fcc structure is largely preserved.
Composition and annealing conditions can affect the nature, size, and distribution of decomposition products.
Excessive precipitation may reduce saturation magnetization.
TEM will be used to assess precipitate presence and size distribution in treated and control samples.
Room-temperature hysteresis measurements will compare coercivity and saturation magnetization between annealed and as-synthesized samples.
Failure to raise coercivity above 100 Oe, or significant degradation of saturation magnetization, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.
